entities.summary:
White Horse Temple, established in 68 AD in Luoyang, Henan, is regarded as the first Buddhist temple in China, marking a pivotal moment in the introduction of Buddhism into East Asia. Founded under the patronage of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dynasty, this temple symbolizes the cultural and religious exchanges between India and China, as well as the beginning of a significant transformation in Chinese spiritual life. Its establishment was motivated by Emperor Ming's reported dream of a golden figure, believed to be the Buddha, which prompted him to seek out Buddhist teachings. 

The temple served as a center for Buddhist learning, attracting monks, scholars, and pilgrims from across Asia. Over the centuries, it became a focal point for the propagation of Buddhism, leading to the establishment of various sects and schools within China. In 220 AD, during the Three Kingdoms period, White Horse Temple was expanded and renovated, further entrenching its role in the religious landscape of China. Its influence was not limited to religious practices but also extended to art, literature, and philosophy, as Buddhist ideas permeated Chinese culture.

The legacy of White Horse Temple is profound; it laid the groundwork for Buddhism to flourish in China, leading to the establishment of other prominent temples and monasteries. The temple has since become a symbol of Sino-Indian cultural exchange, with Buddhism spreading throughout East Asia, influencing societies in Korea, Japan, and beyond. Today, it stands as a testament to the enduring impact of Buddhism on Chinese civilization and serves as a pilgrimage site for Buddhists around the world.
